name: Dental amalgam removal for detox

card.summary: Having silver-colored mercury fillings replaced with other materials in the hope of lowering mercury burden, which proponents link to better energy, clearer skin and a healthier look.
card.aka: Mercury filling removal; amalgam detox; biological dentistry
card.note: Toxicology bodies say removal can raise mercury exposure; the FDA advises against removing sound fillings unless medically necessary.

quick.overview:
Dental amalgam is the grey-silver filling material that contains mercury. In health and bodybuilding circles, some people have their amalgam fillings replaced with composite, glass ionomer or other materials as a detox step, hoping to feel better and, through that, to look better: more energy for training, healthier skin and hair, less puffiness. Replacing a dark filling with a tooth-colored one also changes how the teeth look when smiling.

Proponents point to mercury vapor released from fillings and to individual recovery stories. Regulators and toxicology societies report that amalgam is considered safe for most people and that removal itself can temporarily increase mercury exposure. Large reviews have found insufficient evidence either way for many of the complaints attributed to amalgam.
quick.how: Practitioners of so-called biological or holistic dentistry remove fillings in stages, often with extra suction, rubber dams and breathing apparatus, sometimes alongside supplements or chelation protocols. Forum users describe seeking out a dentist who offers this and note that it can be costly. Some people simply replace amalgam with tooth-colored fillings for cosmetic reasons.
quick.risks: The American College of Medical Toxicology and the American Academy of Clinical Toxicology state that removal of sound fillings is likely to increase mercury exposure and is unnecessary, and they advise against chelation, which carries risks such as kidney injury. The FDA recommends against removal unless medically necessary and advises that high-risk groups such as pregnant women and young children avoid new amalgam. Replacement fillings have their own considerations, including allergy and loss of healthy tooth structure.

lead: Dental amalgam removal for detox is the practice of replacing existing amalgam (silver-mercury) fillings with other materials in order to reduce what proponents regard as a mercury burden on the body.[1] People in the wider health and fitness world who pursue it usually describe the goal as feeling better, with more energy, steadier training and healthier-looking skin and hair, while the swap from dark metal to tooth-colored material also changes the appearance of the smile.

The practice sits inside a long-running dental amalgam controversy. Amalgam was introduced in its modern form in Paris in 1818, and critics have questioned its safety for well over a century.[1] Proponents of removal argue that mercury vapor released from fillings contributes to symptoms ranging from fatigue to neurological complaints; the American Dental Association and the FDA maintain that amalgam is safe for most people.[1]

Research on removal is limited. A 2014 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to support or refute adverse effects of amalgam versus composite, and two randomized trials in children found no significant neuropsychological or kidney differences over five years.[1] Some researchers, such as the German scientist Mutter, have reported improvement in chronic complaints after removal.[1] Discussion in physique-focused forums such as T Nation goes back to at least 2007.[2][3]

chain: Hoped-for energy, skin and training benefits
Tooth-colored fillings also change smile appearance
angle.text: Practitioners hope that reducing mercury exposure improves energy, recovery and complexion, which they connect to a healthier, fitter look. A more direct cosmetic effect is that tooth-colored fillings replace visible dark metal.

infobox: Recommends against removal unless medically necessary[1]

paras: Amalgam fillings combine mercury with other metals and have been used for caries for two centuries; supporters note that they are durable, inexpensive and easy to place.[1] In the detox framing, existing fillings are treated as an ongoing source of low-level mercury vapor, and removal is presented as a step toward lowering a person's total body burden.[1]

Concern about amalgam dates to the 1800s; a theory that oral electrical currents from metal fillings caused symptoms was proposed in 1878 and became popular in Sweden in the 1970s and 1980s.[1] A 1990 broadcast of the US program 60 Minutes triggered a public scare, and the Colorado dentist Hal Huggins, who promoted removal, lost his license in 1996 for unnecessary procedures.[1]

In bodybuilding and nutrition forums, threads such as 'The Mercury DeToxification Thread' (2008) discuss whether mercury from fillings contributes to poor health, with posters noting that it requires a specialized dentist and can be expensive.[2][3]

Critics of amalgam say mercury vapor released from fillings can affect the kidneys and nervous system and contribute to autoimmune disease.[1] Forum posters describe the idea that many people are affected by mercury poisoning and that dentists and regulators are dismissive of it.[2] Some posters observe that people who are health-conscious seem less affected, and that tremors or neurological complaints in older dentists might relate to exposure.[3]

Dentists who offer removal commonly recommend breathing apparatus, high-volume suction and working quickly to limit vapor.[1] Some practitioners combine removal with chelation or supplement protocols; toxicology societies advise against chelation.[1]

A 2004 review found insufficient data to link amalgam to the many complaints attributed to it, and most users had low urinary mercury levels.[1] A 2009 systematic review found no toxic nervous-system effects in children, and a 2014 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to support or refute adverse effects of amalgam or composite.[1] Studies of pregnancy found no negative effects on birth weight, though maternal amalgam correlated with amniotic mercury levels.[1] The researcher Mutter concluded that removal improved chronic complaints in a relevant number of patients.[1]

In 1991 the FDA found no direct hazard from amalgam, classified it as a Class II device in 2009, and in 2020 recommended against its use for high-risk groups: children, pregnant and nursing women, people with neurological disease or kidney impairment, and those sensitive to mercury. It advises against removing existing fillings unless medically necessary.[1] The ADA considers removal for detoxification improper when recommended solely by the dentist.[1] The WHO recommended a global phase-out of dental mercury in 2009, as part of broader mercury reduction.[1] The EU banned amalgam for children under 15 and pregnant or breastfeeding women in 2018 and restricted it further in 2025.[1]

Toxicology societies state that removal likely increases mercury exposure, is unnecessary and is costly, and that chelation can cause kidney injury, dehydration and mineral deficiencies, and can artificially raise urine mercury readings.[1] Replacement materials such as composites carry their own potential risks, including allergies and resin dust exposure.[1]
